The 10 Most Valuable Extended Art Yu-Gi-Oh Cards (So Far!)

Extended art, even more extended prices.

By Ken Nishi

|

Published Sep 18, 2026

|

10 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

2026 has been a momentous year for the Yu-Gi-Oh TCG, with the introduction of Grand Master Rares, major changes to competitive prizing and, perhaps most exciting of all, the long-awaited arrival of extended art cards. While artwork has historically been confined to the square in the center of the card, but extended art cards - referred to as Overframe Rares in the OCG - feature artwork that feels like the monster is jumping out of the card and onto the field!

Extended art cards have been among the most sought-after cards in every set in which they've appeared. They're available as Starlight Rares, which are incredibly difficult to pull but are the ultimate way to bling out your deck. Alternatively, Ultra Rares offer a more affordable option. While they're still relatively difficult to pull, they're a great way to make your deck stand out without spending quite as much.

The Most Valuable Extended Art Yu-Gi-Oh Cards

Here, we're taking a look at the most valuable extended art cards that have been released so far. For the purposes of this article, we aren't going to look at Grand Master Rares. While they technically fall into the extended art category, there have been so few sold listings that it's difficult to determine what their market price really is. That said, Ultra and Starlight Rare extended art cards have quickly become some of the coolest cards to add to a deck or collection. If you're thinking of picking up any of these, they'll certainly cost you a pretty penny!

#10 Mirrorjade the Iceblade Dragon

Starting off the list is Mirrorjade! This card is one of the most important Fusion Monsters for the Branded strategy, providing a key piece of disruption by banishing a monster on the field. With the release of Fallen of the White Dragon earlier this year, plenty of decks have access to this powerhouse.

Mirrorjade's price is tied to its meta performance, and while the deck was extremely popular earlier this year thanks to its solid matchup against Kewl Tune, it has become less popular recently as it struggles against the increasingly popular Light and Darkness Ritual pile decks. Months ago, this card would have placed much higher on this list, but for now, the Starlight Rare's price drop to $450 keeps it down at number 10.

#9 Magician of Dark Chaos - Black Chaos

Up next, we have the latest retrain of Yugi's Magician of Black Chaos! The Magician of Dark Chaos - Black Chaos is a key Ritual monster used in the Light and Darkness Ritual deck, as it provides invaluable removal, returns a Spell card from your Graveyard to hand on summon, and prevents your opponent from destroying or banishing your Spell and Trap cards.

This is the only card on this list from Chaos Origins, the one core set to contain extended art cards so far. However, it has the smallest pool of extended art cards that you can pull from. That means it's mathematically easier to pull the specific Starlight Rare you're looking for! As another meta-relevant card, its price may fluctuate based on how it performs competitively. However, as a retrain of an iconic card, expect it to remain expensive with its $500 price tag, even once the deck has fallen out of the format.

#8 Dominus Impulse

Dominus Impulse is one of the most disruptive Trap cards in the game at the moment! It's able to negate an effect that Special Summons a monster, so you can use it to hit key cards across a wide variety of decks, including Mitsurugi Ritual, Dark Magical Curtain and Kewl Tune Synchro. Of course, it can only be used in decks that consist entirely of Water, Fire and/or Dark monsters. However, if this is a card that your deck is able to run, it's something that you'll definitely make room for!

As a meta-relevant three-of, the Starlight Rare version of Dominus Impulse carries a price tag just over the $500 mark. The card is currently semi-limited in the OCG, but it remains a key card in a ton of different decks in the TCG. Yu-Gi-Oh is a game that's all about disrupting your opponent, and Impulse does exactly that. Expect players to want to keep doing so in style with this card!

#7 Red-Eyes Dark Dragoon

Red-Eyes Dark Dragoon is one of the most iconic Fusion Monsters in Yu-Gi-Oh, combining two of the game's most recognizable monsters into one incredibly powerful boss monster. Dragoon can negate card effects, destroy monsters while dealing damage to your opponent and protect itself from being targeted or destroyed by card effects, making it a formidable threat whenever it hits the field. While it isn't quite the format-defining powerhouse it once was, it has seen a bit of a resurgence recently with the release of Dark Magical Curtain making it much more accessible. 

As one of the most recognizable cards from the game's history, Red-Eyes Dark Dragoon has plenty of collector appeal even when it isn't seeing much competitive play. The Starlight Rare extended art version commands a significant premium, giving collectors a chance to show off one of Yu-Gi-Oh's most famous boss monsters in spectacular fashion. With both nostalgia and competitive history behind it, Dragoon is the kind of card that should remain desirable long after it leaves the competitive spotlight.

#6 Stardust Dragon - Victim Sanctuary

Stardust Dragon is one of the most iconic Synchro Monsters in Yu-Gi-Oh, and Magnificent Monsters gave fans a stunning new version to add to their collections! Stardust Dragon - Victim Sanctuary combines the beloved monster with gorgeous new artwork, making the extended art version feel like Stardust is soaring right off the card. This generic Level 8 Synchro monster will certainly play a significant role for Synchro decks moving forward, as it not only provides a powerful piece of interaction, but also lets you cheat out a "Stardust" Synchro Monster from your Extra Deck! 

Since Magnificent Monsters is one of the newest sets to feature extended art cards, there hasn't been much time for its price to settle. That hasn't stopped collectors from chasing this version of Stardust Dragon, however, and even this early, this card is clearly one of the most desirable cards in the set. Between its iconic status, beautiful artwork, and powerful effect that should remain relevant in future formats, expect Victim Sanctuary to remain as one of the most valuable Starlight Rare extended art cards in the game.

#5 Sky Striker Mecha - Widow Anchor

We're in the top five now, with a couple of Spell cards from one of the most iconic archetypes in Yu-Gi-Oh history. Sky Striker Mecha - Widow Anchor is one of the original Sky Striker Spell cards, and it's still one of their strongest points of interaction, negating the effect of an opponent's monster, and even letting you take control of it if you have three Spells in your Graveyard. The theme has an extremely dedicated player base, and Sky Striker players love to bling out their decks with the highest rarity versions of cards - as you saw with the prices of the Quarter Century Secret Rare alternate art printings of Raye and Roze.

Fortunately, Magnificent Monsters gave us two iconic Sky Striker Spells in extended art form! With art that features both Raye and Roze seeming to jump out of the card, it should be no surprise that this is one of the ultimate chase cards from the set. As a result, we're seeing the card moving at about $650 per copy. If you're a Sky Striker player that wants to continue blinging out your deck, this and the next card are two that you'll definitely be after!

#4 Sky Striker Mobilize - Linkage!

While Widow Anchor represents Sky Striker's ability to disrupt the opponent, Sky Striker Mobilize - Linkage! represents the deck's ability to explode and wipe out the opponent's Life Points all at once. It lets you bring out a Sky Striker Ace monster from your Extra Deck, and can be activated multiple times per turn. With Raye's ability to tag out during the Battle Phase, and Kagari's ability to add this back to hand immediately after using it, Linkage! is a versatile card that can help you get your engine going or win you the game out of nowhere.

Just like Widow Anchor, Linkage! is one of the most iconic cards from the Sky Striker theme. Already a popular strategy, Sky Striker got even more popular after Ryan Yu's iconic 19-0 victory at the North America WCQ earlier this year. Linkage! is a card that every Sky Striker player runs three copies of, so we've seen the early price of the Starlight Rares settle a little higher than that of Widow Anchor, at around $750. Both Widow Anchor and Linkage! as extended arts are amazing ways for Sky Striker fans to bling out one of the game's most iconic strategies.

#3 Dragon Master Magia

Dragon Master Magia is widely regarded as the ultimate chase card in Yu-Gi-Oh, ever since its release as a Quarter Century Secret Rare in Battles of Legend: Terminal Revenge. Similar to Red-Eyes Dark Dragoon, this card is a Fusion monster that combines two of the anime's most iconic cards - Blue-Eyes Ultimate Dragon and Magician of Black Chaos. While Dragon Master Magia does have a powerful effect on the field, it's generally seen as being too difficult to bring out in most competitive decks.

That said, Dragon Master Magia has been a difficult card to pull from packs, regardless of the set. That's no exception with the extended art printing from Battles of Legend: Glorious Gallery! With the three heads of Blue-Eyes appearing to jump off of the card, this art perfectly captures the power that made Kaiba's favorite monster iconic in the first place. Although the Starlight Rare extended art currently sits at number three on the list at $1,150 per copy, we could certainly see this card climb even higher over time.

#2 Dark Magical Curtain

The final two cards on the list are both from Magnificent Monsters! When you think of Dark Magical Curtain, it's easy to assume that the entirety of the card's value comes from the waifu tax, as it features the iconic Dark Magician Girl. However, Dark Magical Curtain is actually an incredibly strong card in its own right, and will likely have a huge impact on the competitive scene for the foreseeable future! It's able to access cards like Witch of the Black Forest and The Gaze of Timaeus, which in turn can fetch Droll & Lock Bird and Red-Eyes Dark Dragoon!

Even so, the collectability of the card should keep its price high long after the Dark Magician cards are no longer meta relevant. The Starlight Rare copies are around $1,150 per copy, placing it firmly at the top end of the most expensive extended art cards released so far. With both competitive players and Dark Magician collectors chasing after it, expect Curtain to maintain its hefty price tag.

#1 Dark Magician, the Pharaoh's Servant

And finally, at the top of the list, we have none other than the retrain of Yugi's signature ace monster - Dark Magician, the Pharaoh's Servant! The retrain gives arguably the most iconic monster in Yu-Gi-Oh's history an amazing new look as well as a powerful effect, letting you wipe out your opponent's backrow as well as access a Dark Magician Spell or Trap card from your Deck.

It should come as no surprise that this card commands an enormous price tag, with the Starlight Rare extended art version currently sitting at around $1,600. This makes Dark Magician, the Pharaoh's Servant, the most valuable extended art card released so far! This card perfectly blends playability, collectability, and nostalgia, and is the type of card that both players and collectors will be chasing after for years to come.

Reality Fracture Limited Magic: The Gathering Set Review: White

Live. Laugh. Gain Life.

By Martin Jůza

|@MartinJuza
|

Published Sep 22, 2026

|

17 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

Welcome to the Set Reviews for Reality Fracture! It's me and Luis Scott-Vargas this time around, and we'll cover every single card that you can open in a Reality Fracture Play Booster. Understanding what you can open is important for Limited, so here's the Play Booster spread for Reality Fracture:

  • 6 Commons, with one replaced by a Special Guests card in 1 out of 55 boosters
  • 1 Uncommon
  • 1 Common or uncommon
  • 3 Echoed-pair cards, including one matching pair of the same rarity
  • 1 Rare or mythic rare
  • 1 Traditional foil card of any rarity
  • 1 Non-foil or traditional foil land, either a basic or common dual land

That's 14 playable cards, plus a token or punch-out counter card. The echoed-pair slots can contain uncommons, rares, or mythics. There's a bunch of Limited archetypes this time around, so here's the recap provided by Wizards of the Coast: 

Reality Fracture Limited Grading Scale

  • Read More: All 3 Reality Fracture Mechanics, Explained
  • Read More: How to Build a Prerelease Deck In Magic: The Gathering

Before I dive into the cards, let's talk about the grading process. Our Limited grading scale is designed to give you a sense of how cards compare to one another, but the grade is less informative than the commentary, so use both to evaluate cards. We use a 0-5 scale, with good commons usually landing around 3.0-3.5 and good rares 4.0 and higher.

  • 5.0: The best of the best, the most powerful cards in the set (such as Fili the Pathfinder or Smaug the Magnificent)
  • 4.5: Incredible Limited card, but just shy of the literal best cards in the set (such as Stone by Sunlight or The Arkenstone)
  • 4.0: A good rare, or top-tier uncommon (Nighthowl Pursuer)
  • 3.5: Top-tier common or good uncommon (The Misty Mountains Cold)
  • 3.0: You basically never cut these (Stir Up Trouble)
  • 2.5: Solid playable that rarely gets cut (Goblin-town Flunkies)
  • 2.0: Decent filler, but sometimes gets cut (Velvetwing Butterflies)
  • 1.5: Pure card filler, which you cut most of the time (Great Fierce Bee)
  • 1.0: Bad filler, which you cut almost all the time (Little Bear)
  • 0.0: Completely unplayable under all circumstances (Wizard's Staff)

Where to Find Reality Fracture Limited Set Reviews

  • Reality Fracture Limited Set Review: Blue

Reality Fracture Limited Set Review: White

Limited: 2.0

 

If your deck is in the market for a combat trick, Academic Ascent can fill the role just fine. The tricky part is adding a planeswalker to your side of the battlefield at instant speed, which will require some extra thought about what you want to leave on defense if you are planning to use it offensively.

Limited: 3.5

 

Ajani Resolute is a cheap planeswalker that takes a while to actually produce a creature, but it is a free lifegain engine which can be really powerful with cards like Unflinching Hortimancer, Bloombrute or Titanbones, Towering Heart.

Not being able to protect himself right away is a big downside though, and lifegain is typically not the strongest build-around mechanic for Limited. I can imagine Ajani being really strong in the right White-Green deck but it seems far from a windmill-slam first pick to me (which mythic planeswalkers often are).

Limited: 4.5

 

Austere Command is a flexible sweeper that can be quite the blowout if timed correctly, letting you either destroy all creatures completely or choose modes that will keep your best creatures alive while removing theirs. Along with the Heartwood tokens, this set features 41 artifacts and enchantments, making the last two modes quite valuable as well.

Limited: 2.5

 

Solid filler which will be good at protecting your Jace token while attacking theirs. Seed Suture adds a little bit of flexibility and a cheap way to activate your lifegain payoffs. I can actually see this card being well-positioned in a planeswalker-focused format.

Limited: 3.5

 

This is a very solid curve-filler that leaves some value behind after it dies. Three power means it can trade up on mana if needed. The downside is being soft to small tokens, but I don't see any common ways of creating 1/1 tokens in this set.

Limited: 1.5 - 3.5

 

Danitha's stats are a bit underwhelming, but it can be a powerful value engine if you can pick up a lot of ways to target creatures you control, like Seed Suture or Predictive Preparations. Worth noting is that there are four equipment cards in the set and only Warrior's Blades is partly in white.

Limited: 4.0

 

I'm always happy to add a cheap lifelinker to my deck and Enlightened Confidant has strong synergy with the passive lifegain effects in this format. Typically, the Confidant will net you a free land from surveil if you gained one life with something like a Seed Suture or Koth of the Homestead. Because of the weaker stats, I wouldn't expect Enlightened Confidant to connect too often in combat and treat it as an upgraded Dark Confidant. Even if you only get one or two cards with this over the course of the game, the Confidant has already done more than enough.

Draft: 2.0
Sealed: 2.5

 

The stats are a bit underwhelming for a five-drop, but there are 95 cards with the legendary subtype in Reality Fracture, which makes Fateshaper Aspirant a reasonable filler card with some flexibility.

Limited: 1.0 - 3.5

 

Flickering Hound can be a powerful value engine, but investing four mana into a 2/2 creature with no immediate effect on the board is a significant loss in momentum. You really want your deck to be full of value-producing creatures who enter "prepared" or have good "enter the battlefield" abilities to take full advantage of it. White offers five prepared creatures with either Seed Suture or Peer Review, so the potential for a nice setup is certainly there. That said, don't let the rare symbol on this card trick you into thinking you should automatically put it into every white deck.

Limited: 3.0

 

Generous Revival can be a nice two-for-one in the right scenario if you are bringing back synergy pieces or against a deck full of removal. However, it can also be awkward to use if your opponent dealt with your creatures with bounce or exile effects or if you didn't get to trade early. I am typically not a fan of situational cards like this one, but this synergizes really well with surveil by both adding more creatures to the graveyard and having flashback.

Limited: 0.0

 

This card does absolutely nothing without a way to gain life in the same turn, which is the lowest possible floor, a total blank. This isn't Modern Constructed where you can pitch Autochthon Wurm to create 15 tokens with it on turn three. Other than a big creature with lifelink, I don't really see any reliable ways to gain at least three or more life while keeping three mana up to cast this at the same time. Way too situational for my tastes.

Limited: 4.0

 

The discard ability is a cheap bit of interaction against an attacking or blocking creature and there will be times the main static ability will be relevant. This set features Cadet tokens from Peer Review and cards like Hexhaven Battalion, Saheeli, Consul of Oversight or The Theorist, Jace Beleren, making Gideon's Memorial a nice yet flexible card.

Limited: 2.5

 

Ghalta is effectively a 7/7, though worth noting is that it works very poorly with any fight spells. You need a four toughness creature to make her cost five, which is a very solid deal and even if you are paying six mana, it is still a reasonable cost. This is a decent curve-topper if you need one, but not something I would pick super highly because expensive creatures are typically quite easy to come by and you can only afford to play so many of them in Limited.

Limited: 2.25

 

Graft Surgeon seems like a fine curve-filler that has nice synergy with Seed Suture and all the many ways in this format that let you add +1/+1 counters on your creatures like Predictive Preparations or Emergency Phytomedic.

Limited: 4.5

 

Guiding Hydra being a repeatable way to buff your board with a flexible mana cost seems like a great deal, with an extra upside that even if you don't have any other creatures, you can play it as a big standalone threat. There are lots of cards that can add more counters to it and is quite splashable. Seems very strong to me.

Draft: 2.0 - 2.5
Sealed: 2.5

 

Six power and six toughness worth of stats split across three bodies with an extra planeswalker on top can be a strong card in the right deck, or even in the right matchup where your opponent has a lot of one-for-one removal. At this stage of the game, you typically prefer a 6/6 body over three smaller ones, but if your deck is looking to go wide, it can be an upside. It is quite expensive in mana, but landcycling gives it nice utility otherwise. I'd expect to play the first copy about 50% of the time depending on my deck and mana curve.

Limited: 2.0 - 4.0
Draft: 1.5 - 3.0
Sealed: 2.5 - 4.0

 

Seven mana is a lot to pay even for a sweeper and Kindred Judgment is going to require some serious setting up because of overlapping creature types between your and your opponent's board. At first glance, it seems quite clunky to me but the format might be slow enough where this ends up being good enough. Still, it is a card that can win you the game out of nowhere and they aren't easy to find in Limited. I'd expect it to perform better in Sealed compared to Draft, which tends to be much faster. Either way, this should be a really good sideboard card.

Limited: 4.0

 

Koth is both a lifegain and a value engine combined, which is really strong for a cheap creature. The +1/+1 counters are unfortunately limited only to Plains and not just any land, but even one trigger already makes this worthwhile. Being able to distribute the counters anywhere is going to steadily improve your board while enjoying the overlapping synergies.

Limited: 2.5 - 4.0

 

Liliana the Faultless is an upgraded iteration of Soul Warden, which isn't typically a good Limited card because the stats are too poor for it to meaningfully matter in combat. That said, lifegain is quite relevant in this format and combined with the ability to protect other creatures or planeswalkers, this makes her a very reasonable card to play. The rare symbol doesn't mean Liliana should automatically go into every deck, but you don't need much more than a few copies of a common card like Unflinching Hortimancer to make her quite good.

Limited: 0.0 - 1.5

 

This set features eight planeswalkers and that is an unusually high number, though keep in mind that only one of them is white. Loyal Tutor is a card disadvantage, but planeswalkers are usually so powerful that you should be able to make up for it.

Does that mean you should always play Loyal Tutor if you have a planeswalker? I wouldn't say so because you can always draw the planeswalker naturally and then you end up with a card that does absolutely nothing. I would include the card in situations where the planeswalker is completely busted, or perhaps a key synergy piece in my deck and ideally I also have some ways to replace the card with something that creates card advantage instead.

Limited: 4.0

 

Lyra is a great card no matter how much lifegain or how many Angels you have, because the baseline stats of 3/3 flying for three mana is already well ahead of the curve. That said, there are only three Angels in the entire set, so don't expect to play a dedicated typal deck anytime soon. Lyra is easy to trigger, good to play early, and really good to play late.

Limited: 3.5

 

Creatures keep getting better and better, especially by creating immediate value in some way when they enter the battlefield. This makes one-for-one removal at sorcery speed nowhere near as impactful when you were mostly using it to answer Serra Angel or Shivan Dragon. Still, I'm of course not going to ignore an exile effect that deals with any permanent, especially in a highly synergistic set such as this one. Do keep in mind that the dynamic has shifted recent years, though.

Limited: 3.0

 

Travel Preparations was one of the best cards in Innistrad Limited. Although the flashback cost on Predictive Preparations has now doubled, and this is a big difference. Still, I expect this card to be quite good in aggressive decks and has a nice synergy with surveil, as you can put the card in the graveyard while still getting value from it.

Limited: 3.5

 

Two mana to destroy a creature is an excellent rate. Typically in Limited, you can only achieve this by answering an attacking creature, but Prophesied End lets you do this outside of combat but with a real drawback. Still, being able to remove a high-value creature is usually worth it and you would much rather have the choice than not. Keep in mind that you can target your own creatures, possibly cashing it in in response to a removal spell or by eating a token or something with a powerful leaves-the-battlefield effect.

Mainboard: 0.5
Sideboard: 3.0

 

Refute Destiny is an excellent sideboard card and I even remember some unbalanced formats where a card like Deathmark was a reasonable mainboard inclusion, especially if your deck had some draw and discard effects. Exiling the permanent is a really nice upside, too.

Limited: 4.0

 

Two-drop with stats ahead of the curve and creates a planeswalker token when it attacks? Sign me up!

Limited: 1.0 - 2.5

 

A combination of weak stats and not being able to use the ability on my opponent's turn makes Rescue Girl, First Responder useful in very specific decks with a bunch of high value and/or cheap creatures with good "enters the battlefield" abilities. I can also see her activated ability coming in handy against a deck with a lot of aura-based removal like Infinite Coursework. Rescue Girl seems too situational and mana consuming to me. However, it does give you a cheap way to attack Jace tokens in the air which isn't nothing.

Limited: 0.5

 

You are going to be surveilling often due to the Empower Jace mechanic, so the potential to set up a loaded graveyard is definitely there if the format is slow enough. But nine mana is just way too much to reliably get to in Limited these days. Even in a scenario where you survive long enough to make your ninth land drop or get there with ramp effects before then, your creatures may have been exiled or enchanted with cards like Infinite Coursework, so you are still not even guaranteed to reap the full value from this.

Limited: 4.0

 

Good stats combined with a value engine makes Saheeli a strong card, especially in a format where having Jace tokens grants you consistent ways to surveil (and thus creating you Thopter tokens).

Limited: 2.0

 

Shatterwing Pegasus looks like a classic medium filler to me in a regular Limited format. Stats are below rate and the activation cost seems pricey, although having a mana sink adds extra value. The card becomes much better if there is a go-wide strategy, but the one big upside is that cheap flyers should be good in a format where everyone has a low-loyalty planeswalker on the battlefield most of the time.

Limited: 3.0

 

As far as conditional removal spells go, Surgical Precision is amazing because it will never rot in your hand if your opponent doesn't have a target. It can still be a bit too situational or slow for Traditional Draft depending on the speed of the format. With Sealed, you never cut cards like this one. Don't forget that Seed Suture lets you target your opponents creatures as well, which can be a nice way to take down a high-value creature with less than four power.

Limited: 4.25

 

Teyo can protect your permanent from a removal spell, help your creature win combat, and even add a loyalty counter on a planeswalker; that's some excellent utility for just two mana. Now the best part — if you want to curve out, he can even put the counter on himself and come down as a 2/2 with flash that can potentially ambush another creature, which means Teyo comes with a high floor and is incredibly versatile.

Limited: 3.0

 

The stats on Thalia, the Survivor are unexciting for a four-drop, but lifelink can help you stabilize a racing situation or repeatedly enable lifegain payoffs. Taxing your opponent's spells is quite relevant, especially with so many prepared creatures in the format. Strong synergy with counters from Seed Suture. It looked a bit unexciting upon first glance, but after considering the format, I like Thalia quite a bit.

Limited: 3.5

 

Tomik looks very strong to me. A flying two-drop that lets you pressure your opponent's Jace token while the attacking restriction helps you keep yours around. Jumping a creature with a +1/+1 counter can enable some bigger swings in the late-game. Tomik is effective both early and late.

Limited: 2.25

 

White seems to have a fair amount of lifegain in this format and especially Seed Suture synergizes nicely with Unflinching Hortimancer, potentially turning it into a much bigger threat for just one more mana.

Limited: 3.75

 

On the one hand, the ability to turn loyalty counters into creatures is very powerful and helps you protect your planeswalker. A good way to look at Way of the Healer is that it effectively changes your Jace from "(-1): surveil 1" to "(-2): surveil 1 and create a 2/2 token". That's a massive upgrade.

On the other hand, if you are behind and need to play this on turn four with no other creatures, your opponent kills your Cadet token and deals with your Jace by attacking, that doesn't sound nearly as exciting. I believe this card is quite powerful, but it requires some planning ahead to reap the most value out of it.

Limited: 2.0

 

Way of the Mentor can be strong in a dedicated lifegain setup, but it's not something I would play in every white deck. I like that the card immediately replaces itself, but it doesn't provide you with a way to defend the Jace token, making it quite the situational card.

Limited: 2.5

 

Yoshimaru, Beloved Companion is a slow synergy piece and an expensive mana sink, but the fact it's incredible with Predictive Preparations alone makes me believe he is going to be quite good in the correct deck.

Limited: 2.0 - 3.5

 

Yuriko, Blade of the Mighty is a very expensive way to repeatedly grant your attacker with double strike. This can be decent if your deck has a lot of creatures with flying, lifelink, or ways to consistently make one big attacker. The combat restriction should usually be an upside, but it works both ways, meaning it can turn off your own tricks as well. You shouldn't put Yuriko in every deck (especially when you are on the draw), but it can be effective.

Limited: 3.5

 

If I understand the wording correctly, the mana value restriction applies to both the creature and the planeswalker, which makes it a lot worse than if it could kill any creature. The Jace token being zero mana value is not ideal. You should always find a good target for it and often trade up on mana, but situations where you are staring down a Repurposed Enforcer or Ajani Resolute while being unable to use your removal spell is going to feel really bad.

Top 5 White Limited Commons From Reality Fracture

White seems good to me, mostly because it features four removal spells that each cost only one white pip. I can see it being a very popular color in Sealed because you can easily splash for the removal spells. Here's my rankings for the best white commons in the set:

  1. Memory Trap
  2. Campus Crier
  3. Surgical Precision
  4. Predictive Preparations
  5. Blossom-Blessed Angel

For Sealed, I would probably put Surgical Precision above Crier, which I would expect to perform better in a faster Traditional Draft environment. Fateshaper Aspirant is also going to be much better in Sealed than in Draft and would probably jump to fourth or fifth here. Similarly, Hexhaven Battalion deserves an extra boost in Sealed because of its flexibility.

Reality Fracture Limited Magic: The Gathering Set Review: Blue

Empowering Jace has never been easier.

By Luis Scott-Vargas

|@lsv
|

Published Sep 22, 2026

|

9 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

Welcome to the Set Reviews for Reality Fracture! It's me and Martin Jůza this time around, and we'll cover every single card that you can open in a Reality Fracture Play Booster. Understanding what you can open is important for Limited, so here's the Play Booster spread for Reality Fracture:

  • 6 Commons, with one replaced by a Special Guests card in 1 out of 55 boosters
  • 1 Uncommon
  • 1 Common or uncommon
  • 3 Echoed-pair cards, including one matching pair of the same rarity
  • 1 Rare or mythic rare
  • 1 Traditional foil card of any rarity
  • 1 Non-foil or traditional foil land, either a basic or common dual land

That's 14 playable cards, plus a token or punch-out counter card. The echoed-pair slots can contain uncommons, rares, or mythics. There's a bunch of Limited archetypes this time around, so here's the recap provided by Wizards of the Coast: 

Reality Fracture Limited Grading Scale

  • Read More: All 3 Reality Fracture Mechanics, Explained
  • Read More: How to Build a Prerelease Deck In Magic: The Gathering

Before I dive into the cards, let's talk about the grading process. Our Limited grading scale is designed to give you a sense of how cards compare to one another, but the grade is less informative than the commentary, so use both to evaluate cards. We use a 0-5 scale, with good commons usually landing around 3.0-3.5 and good rares 4.0 and higher.

  • 5.0: The best of the best, the most powerful cards in the set (such as Fili the Pathfinder or Smaug the Magnificent)
  • 4.5: Incredible Limited card, but just shy of the literal best cards in the set (such as Stone by Sunlight or The Arkenstone)
  • 4.0: A good rare, or top-tier uncommon (Nighthowl Pursuer)
  • 3.5: Top-tier common or good uncommon (The Misty Mountains Cold)
  • 3.0: You basically never cut these (Stir Up Trouble)
  • 2.5: Solid playable that rarely gets cut (Goblin-town Flunkies)
  • 2.0: Decent filler, but sometimes gets cut (Velvetwing Butterflies)
  • 1.5: Pure card filler, which you cut most of the time (Great Fierce Bee)
  • 1.0: Bad filler, which you cut almost all the time (Little Bear)
  • 0.0: Completely unplayable under all circumstances (Wizard's Staff)

Where to Find Reality Fracture Limited Set Reviews

  • Reality Fracture Limited Set Review: White

Reality Fracture Limited Set Review: Blue

Limited: 3.0

 

I don't mind a Cancel with upside, and this can both cost less and give you some good value thanks to the Empower Jace ability. One thing to note is this does encourage you to cast your spells before attacking, because if the opponent has Countersculpt, you want to be able to attack the Jace token.

Limited: 0.0

 

This is way too situational to be worth running. It draw you zero or one card most of the time, which doesn't come close to making it worth it for the times you draw five.

Limited: 2.5

 

Cryotheory Adept is a nice way to apply pressure, and even gives you one last push from the graveyard. I don't mind this for aggressive decks, but I would mostly avoid it if you are playing a more controlling archetype.

Limited: 3.5

 

Diviner of Victory isn't a Limited bomb, but it is going to contribute nicely to the predicted victories. A 1/1 with prowess for one that comes with a momentum-creating spell is awesome, and I'd be happy to first-pick this. It's best in assertive decks, but great anywhere else.

Limited: 2.0

 

Divining Duelist will always find something to do, but it will rarely be awesome. This is the definition of filler, and like some of these other cards, does better in faster games. It's an infinite combo with Splinter Twin which may come up in Limited, though.

Limited: 3.0

 

In exchange for your Essence Scatter not working as well in the late game, you gain the ability to counter legendary non-creatures and use it as a peculiar combat trick. That all sounds fine to me, and is as good as Essence Scatter at least (which is to say, a solid common).

Limited: 3.5

 

Blue really doesn't get much better removal than this, so I don't think you're going to pass on it all that often. Locking the creature down and losing all abilities handles most everything, with the biggest drawback being enchantment removal or bounce to free the perennial student. I also love the "it becomes unprepared" text, even though I think it's just flavor here.

Limited: 3.5

 

Making an eight loyalty Jace at the end of turn and immediately drawing a card is sweet, especially because the next thing you get to do is untap and activate Jace again. Two cards and a Jace token at two loyalty is not bad for three mana, and this goes especially hard if you have any of the other Jace payoffs.

Limited: 3.5

 

This has to be in the running for one of the top commons in Reality Fracture — as you get a 2/1, a card, and a Jace on one loyalty all just for three mana (I suppose you don't have to use the Jace to draw, but I assume you will most of the time). I'm seeking as many of these as I can get, and don't think there's really a cap on how many you should play.

Limited: 2.0

 

This kind of combat trick often falls flat, though 4/5 is starting to get big enough that it's worth it. It also can shrink a massive creature, and the combination of the two abilities makes this reasonable for any aggressive deck.

Limited: 3.5

 

I like the setup for the grindier games, where every turn you get a free surveil (or work towards drawing a card). Plan for All Outcomes also really pays you off for playing instants, as you can empower Jace on both your turn and theirs.

Limited: 1.0 // 3.5

 

I wouldn't mainboard any of the cards in this cycle (unless Sealed proves to be particularly lop-sided in color balance), but they add some good options for Traditional Draft. Precise Redaction is great out of the sideboard, and worth it if the opponent is in either white or black.

Limited: 2.5

 

Protege's Awakening is a powerful card draw engine, netting you two cards and three life at a minimum. If you can defend Jace, you get even more value, and in the right deck this can do good work. It is a bit clunky, so not every deck will be interested in this.

Limited: 4.0

 

I don't think I've seen a card packed with this much value in quite some time. Nothing here is flashy, there is just a lot of it — two instances of drawing and discarding, two instances of stun counters, a 2/2 body, and two more cards. Seasoned Cyromancer looks incredible and will be very high pick for me.

Limited: 3.0

 

Class is eternally in session here, as this gives you a lot to do with your mana. It smoothes out your draws, creates a token, and can surveil again. There's never a dull moment with this card, but copies beyond the first do go down in value quite a bit.

Limited: 4.5

 

Sphinx of False Conclusions is just flat-out incredible. Not only do you get a four-power flier with a decent attack trigger, it just comes back for free (albeit once). There is basically no way besides a counterspell to interact with this favorably, and it asks nothing of you besides that you cast it for it to be great.

Limited: 1.0

 

I love me a Divination (more than most, even), but double-blue and single blue are not in the same league for this kind of spell. Sphinx's Approach doesn't help draw you a fourth land unless you have double-Island, and the Sphinx text is essentially meaningless in Limited.

Limited: 3.0

 

Surveillance Phantasm basically justifies itself without any help, and becomes even better when it's in the right deck. I like how well this plays defense, and if you absolutely need to clock damage with it, you can do so.

Limited: 4.5

 

Every mode on this is a threat, and there are a lot of modes. The Theorist, Jace Beleren gives you a steady stream of cards and plenty of interaction to keep that stream going, making it a fantastic card for Limited. This does do better when you have a developed battlefield, so try and play to that in order to set Jace up the best possible outcome.

Limited: 3.5

 

I'd pretty happily play an 0/3 that Empowers Jace for three without any other text, much less flash and the anti-counter ability. Granted, those don't actually add up to much, but Theorist's Proxy replacing itself right away makes it an easy inclusion.

Limited: 3.0

 

I love when the landcyclers are good cards to play, and Undulating Witness hits a great note. It's strong enough to be worth casting coupled with landcycling to make it flexible. It's not busted per se, but it makes your deck run a little more smoothly.

Limited: 3.0

 

Time is a flat circle in the Echoverse and Unsummon is good once more, many years after it first saw the light of day. One mana is just cheap enough to make up for being down a card, as the momentum you gain by bouncing an expensive creature gives you a real advantage on the battlefield. This can also save your own creatures, and even re-trigger enter the battlefield abilities in a pinch.

Limited: 3.5

 

I'd play a 2/3 flying prowess in most blue decks, so getting the Arc of Fortune option is a nice bonus. You won't want to cast this too often, but if you can throw your hand and cast it while they have more cards, you do end up ahead. It's a bit win-more, but that's just how prowess cards roll these days.

Limited: 3.5

 

Flesh Duplicate is here for a good time, not a long time. As long as you copy a high-impact creature, you can usually get a card's worth of value one way or another before this vanishes. Two mana is cheap enough that this will almost always end up being a great deal.

Limited: 1.0 // 3.0

 

Consign to Memory is another sideboard card, as it won't come up enough to make it worth mainboarding unfortunately.

Limited: 4.0

 

Six mana is pricey, but the effects you get with Sublime Epiphany are numerous and strong. The most common time to play this is while they are casting a spell, as picking up the counter mode plus everything else usually swings the game sufficiently enough to win. Still, there's no wrong way to go about things, as picking a bunch of modes is powerful enough regardless.

Limited: 3.0

 

Consider makes your deck a little more consistent, but isn't a high priority unless you are really going deep on prowess synergies.

Top 5 Blue Limited Commons From Reality Fracture

With the ratings for blue wrapped up, here's my rankings for the best commons in the color for Reality Fracture Limited:

  1. Mindseeker Oculus
  2. Infinite Coursework
  3. Icy Reception
  4. Semester Foreseer
  5. Unsummon

Blue has some very nice commons, with Undulating Witness being in the conversation as well. The combination of card advantage and speed is a nice one to have, and blue seems like it's doing quite well for itself in Reality Fracture Limited.

Disney Lorcana|news

Everything We Learned From The Hyperia City Lorecast

Get Hype(ria)

By Jason Grabher-Meyer

|

Published Sep 22, 2026

|

16 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

Another massive Lorecast live stream has come and gone, and in terms of sheer card count, this might be the biggest one Ravensburger's ever unleashed! We just saw a boat load of new cards from Disney Lorcana's upcoming Hyperia City release, arriving October 16 at Disney Parks and local game stores worldwide. If you missed it, we're here to make sure you're filled in on all the reveals.

…But before we get there, let's take a moment to discuss the release that's actually coming first - and the surprise event that's supporting it.

The Great Hunny Rescue Is Almost Here!

Yes, The Great Hunny Rescue - the new Illumineer's Quest that debuted at Gen Con in August - will finally be available worldwide on October 2, priced at an MSRP of $59.99.

In addition, stores will be able to host play events for The Great Hunny Rescue, awarding a promo version of If I Didn't Have You from Attack of the Vine, and an exclusive Hunny Wizard lore counter. You won't want to miss these if you're a fan of Monsters, Inc. or Winnie the Pooh in all his Disney Lorcana forms, so reach out to your local game store and find out when you can participate.

Hyperia City Reveals

The main event of each quarterly Lorecast is always the extended look into the featured release, and today's stream did not disappoint. Hyperia City launches at Disney Parks and authorized Ravensburger Playhub stores on October 16, followed by a global release on October 23.

As Disney fans in the know had guessed, Hyperia City channels Disney's roots, inspired by Hyperion Studios - the home of Disney Animation from 1926 to 1940. The vibe is a mix of art deco and art nouveau: think Old Hollywood, and all the images of glitz, glam, and gold that come with it.

Want details? Well, Hyperia City is Disney Lorcana's most fully realized setting yet. Don't believe me? Every Prerelease Box will actually come with a full map of the city! The map details some of the Locations you'll find in the actual set and gives you a good idea of how each ink is going to manifest in this chapter of the Lorcana story.

The post cards and mini posters in previous prelease kits were fun, but for longtime Disney parks fans like me, this is really scratching that itchy nostalgia we have for old school fold-out paper maps of Disney World and Disneyland. It's going to catch a lot of us Disney adults right in the feels. And while you're squinting at the image above, be sure to check out those dice that come with the kit as well - looks like marbled silver material with gold accents? Very on-theme.

But of course, the best value-add in every prerelease kit is the exclusive promo card, and as usual each of these kits will come with one of six gold-bordered promos, stamped with the set name. These have proven really popular with collectors since their debut in Wilds Unknown, and this time around there are some really promising cards in the mix that could make a big impact - in both your prerelease sealed deck, and competition afterward.

Amber gets Nick Wilde - Inquisitive Harbormaster, a 6-drop that really plays best Shift in for 4 ink. The ability to Shift Nick on Turn 4 or earlier, immediately quest for 3 lore, and then send whatever opposing character that might threaten Nick off on a quest next turn by way of the new Adventurous keyword is actually pretty good. I could definitely see this raking in 6 lore pretty often before opponents can deal with it. That said, if we're talking about 3-lore questers here the real star may be Merlin - Ink Drop Tinkerer, Shifting in for 5 ink but immediately giving you 2 Ink Drops. It's like playing a 6/8 3-lore quester for 3 ink total. Seems good.

Fans of A Goofy Movie get not one, but two promos to chase, starting with Above the Crowd. A mid-costed song that can eliminate an opposing character in the most permanent way possible - without inking it, returning it to the opponent's hand, or leaving it in the discard for recursion - is definitely useful. And the Dreamborn Goody - Dancing Superstar is a potential build-around for new song-centric decks, helping all your Singers close out games faster with extra lore. If you liked the Goofy Movie cards in Fabled but just couldn't quite get the deck to work (like me), you've got a ton of new cards coming your way, and these two are just some of the examples we saw in the Lorecast. Read on!

Finally, Judy Hopps - Day Camp Instructor is early game Sapphire ramp with a cost of 2, which is sure to give some of us traumatic flashbacks. Unless you have an Ink Drop to help play a character before you play Judy, you probably won't be able to leverage her effect on your second turn, but her potential seems off the charts. This may be the best promo of the bunch. And finally, Berlioz - Tiny Rascal just nips any character for damage when it hits play, an effect I'm not sure I've seen on an inkable 1-drop before. Dumptruck just got dunked on.

For many of us, the big pulls we'll be looking for at those prerelease events are going to be new Legendary cards, and Ravensburger spoiled us with a look at more than half of the set's Legendary cards.

The first two reveals are cards we're partially familiar with from product packaging - both Baymax - Amped Up and Madam Mim - Resourceful Trickster appear in the Hyperia City 2-Player Starter Set. But now we can finally see them in all their glory, and both cards look really good: You can Shift Baymax anytime you have two Ink Drops to burn, and from there he's a 5/8 that turns all of your Ink Drop generating effects into hard inkwell ramp instead. That could be amazing with the right Shift targets and the right Ink drop effects. Meanwhile Mim feels like the evolution of Ursula - Power Hungry from The First Chapter, a big purple body that quests for 3 lore and gives immediate draw power. The kicker? Mim gives two draws on play instead of one, provided you used an Ink Drop to pay for her, and then she's a once-per-turn draw engine. Seems Nutty.

From there we saw three Legendary characters that all revolve around songs. Ravensburger's told us that Hyperia City will feature Singers and songs more than most sets, and these three cards show that they mean business: Powerline - Megastar is Singer 9, gets back Singers from your discard, and makes bigger and bigger quests the more Singers you control. You can see the immediate potential with that new Ruby Goofy. Meanwhile Aurora is a low cost Princess that gets back songs you just used on play, and then does the same routine as Alan-A-Dale - Rockin' Rooster from Shimmering Skies. Again, it's another song support card that helps you finish games faster.

Finally, my favorite reveal from the entire Lorecast was Max Goof - Karaoke Star. How is this card not busted? Trading a song you don't need to draw two cards is good enough on a 3-cost body, but later in the game Max starts questing for a whopping 4 lore as well - ridiculous. I'm playing this card in something come October, just watch.

Finally we saw not one, but two Steel Legendaries. Shere Khan grants the ability to challenge ready characters; that's an effect that's historically pretty expensive in Lorcana, but it feels affordable here on a 4-ink character. Combined with Shere Khan's ability to turn challenges into free Ink Drops once per turn and you've got a card that's worth a serious look. And then Steel gets perhaps the best Location support character yet in Tiana - Party Hostess. She's not cheap at a regular play cost of 7 ink or Shift 5, but a free "Draw 2, Discard 1" is always good. Then the kicker - if you discarded a Location you get to play it for free. This card is going to do something really good, at some point in the future.

Looking beyond the Legendary cards there are some big highlights, and some very cool design work in both card mechanics and artwork. Case in point…

Remember Me is the kind of card art that you appreciate more the longer you look at it. It's The Black Cauldron or The Horned King in song form, and that could give a ton of longevity to a quick Amber song deck that stays low to the ground. Cauldron and Horned King are both much slower in unlocking your discard, and they're both uninkable. To see this effect on a more searchable, potentially much faster card is really interesting.

Then there's Port Authority - Center Hub, which demonstrates Amber's "Ink Drops are for everyone" kind of sharing approach to the Ink Drop mechanic. At 8 willpower and 2 lore per turn, it's better than it looks at first glance.

Over in Amethyst Mama Coco gets some sick-ass Hyperian wheels, while Merlin is getting you an Ink Drop - pretty good - and then questing for 2 and giving you a free draw every turn. The Merlin's obviously going to see play and screams Emerald Amethyst. Meanwhile I'm not sure what could use Higitus Figitus, which seems over costed for what it does without drawing you a card in compensation. But hey, maybe if you're feeding Ink Drops to characters like Madam Mim you won't mind.

Of course Emerald gets a new Go Go Tomago that's really good. Why wouldn't they… Be ready to see this card all over the place in annoyingly fast green decks. Meanwhile Honey Lemon - Testing the Limits is just Hiram Flaversham - Toymaker again, with some already calling it the most broken card of the set; and Another Tale to Spin probably isn't good, but does have me humming the Talespin theme song. Which is actively making my Tuesday even better.

Ernesto De La Cruz is a terrifying skeleton that eats singing children right off the table, which is absolutely perfect for the character. Singer 8 is no joke, too, and the artwork is some of my favorite from the set so far. I lowkey love this thing. And Wasabi - Called Into Battle is just sort of a better, or at least much easier, version of Mulan - Elite Archer? I'm down. I always loved that version of Mulan, but making her work consistently was next to impossible. Wasabi's a great new take on a failed-but-promising mechanic from days gone by.

Arthur - Novice Blacksmith is… fine? I guess? It doesn't seem like a must play at first blush but I feel like there could be some tricks here, some synergies with other cards. (Yes, it can work with that Amethyst Merlin; no, that doesn't impress me. I'm thinking there's something bigger.) What DOES impress me though, is Jousting Match, breaking the 5-damage barrier that Steel's struggled with since the rotation of And Then Along Came Zeus with the condition of using an Ink Drop to pay for it. At a cost of 3 it could definitely see play if Steel and its companion inks get enough reasonable Ink Drop generators.

And finally, Cinderella - Unintentional Icon is the only non-promo Sapphire card we saw revealed, and our second of two Iconic cards in the release! I don't think this card would be very impressive if Cinderella - Dream Come True didn't exist. But it does, so Unintentional Icon has obvious play potential. And it's going to look awesome with Iconic foiling.

We also learned some things about Ink Drops along the way, complete with a look at two of the Ink Drop token cards (which don't count as cards, to be accurate), that you'll find in packs. While we only got to see two of these there will assumedly be one for each ink, representing the different approaches to Ink Drops that will characterize each color. Expect unique Ink Drop strategies in all six hues.

In addition, we got confirmation of a few basic facts. First, Etienne Bonin, Senior Play Designer for Hyperia City confirmed that there's no limit to how many Ink Drops you can spend per turn. Spend one, spend them all, it's up to you. Bonin also confirmed that these Ink Drop tokens will appear in the bonus / puzzle / marketing slot of Hyperia City boosters; they won't take up a regular card slot. That's good. Sadly we also learned that there won't be foil Ink Drop cards - at least not yet - which feels like a missed opportunity. One Piece players absolutely love foiling out their DON!! cards, and as a Lorcana fan I'm itching to ride the same dopamine wave.

Finally, we got a look at all of the promo cards supporting the set, and then some…

Minnie Mouse - Urbani Visionary is the Buy-A-Box promo given for purchasing a booster box, at Ravensburger Playhub stores, while supplies last. Donald Duck - Taxi Driver is the "seasonal" promo you'll find at conventions and big events like Disney Lorcana Challenges, and Nick Wilde - Providing Backup is the Collection Quest promo, as in-store Collection Quests return to stores! People liked them, and it's nice to see Ravensburger's keeping them going.

The League Play promos for the season are Everyone Knows Juanita, which I can't imagine not seeing play; Tramp - Quick on His Feet, a flexible Rush character in Ruby; and that Arthur again.

Baymax fans will want to get their prerelease product at Disney Parks and participating Disney Store locations, because if they do they'll score this sweet Baymax - Lab Assistant card, the next in the Magical Places promo series. And this nonfoil version of Minnie Mouse - Amethyst Champion is a gorgeous alt art reprint of the Whispers in the Well original; this will be given in a mid-season event at Ravensburger Playhub stores, with the foil version available at the World Championship in December. Think Promo A Whole New World.

And finally, the Set Championship promo card for Hyperia City is none other than Honey Lemon - Testing the Limits! This seems like a fantastic pick, a fan-favorite Big Hero 6 character with tremendous playability and a ton of hype from the competitive crowd. The 1st Place playmat at Set Champs will also feature the same artwork of Honey Lemon, matching the promo card.

Yes, Ravensburger revealed more than 40 different cards from Hyperia City and the supporting promo lineup in this Lorecast. Whew. I'm tuckered out, but hugely excited.

2027 Releases: Inkdark, Wall-E, and Pixie Hollow

While the bulk of the Lorecast was devoted to that massive pile of preview cards, we also got some news about the next three sets. Including some huge info for next year's first release, Into the Inkdark.

Yes, that is the second Illustrious Rare that the luckiest among us may find in Collector's Boosters of Into The Inkdark - the classic Rise of the Floodborn card, The Queen - Commanding Presence, with incredible new art from Arch Apolar, serialized to just 23 copies, and… a new name? Yes, looks like the Illustrious version of this card will restore The Evil Queen to the name we're all a little more familiar with.

We also got to see part a new Location card, The Dark Illuminary - Hades's Stronghold, which is basically one giant teaser for the storyline twists we'll encounter in the set. And on top of that we got a look at one more Into The Inkdark highlight…

She's back! Sort of! We don't know what this smaller-sized version of the giant-sized Tinker Bell does, but the illustration along is going to make this a popular pull.

Beyond all that we learned two big points about Into the Inkdark: First, that the set will hit shelves at Disney Parks and local game stores on February 5, followed by a wide release on February 12; and the actual MSRP of those Collector's Boosters. Individual packs will have a suggested price of 34.99 USD / 34.99 EU / 31.99 GBP / 44.99 CAD, and a full 12-pack display box is suggested to retail at 419.88 USD / 419.88 EU / 383.88 GBP / 539.88 CAD.

And last up, we got a glimpse of the next two sets releasing in 2027.

We already knew the name and Q2 release of Cosmic Quest, but what had not been confirmed is the glory pictured above: The Disney Lorcana debut of Wall-E. As the year-later follow-up to Wilds Unknown it makes sense to center this set around another of Pixar's biggest properties, and Disney fandom is sure to show out for this one.

And last up, the third set of the year arriving in Q3 appears to be themed around Tinker Bell and her companions from Pixie Hollow! This is a bit of a deep cut for a lot of Disney fans, but a huge hit for the ones that love this license, or have kids who do. We'll have to wait and see what other characters may take center stage in this release but for now, it looks like Giant Tink may be getting some backup.

Those sets are still a long ways off, but with The Great Hunny Rescue and Hyperia City both arriving in the next few weeks, Octobers going to be an awesome month for Disney Lorcana! Don't forget to call your locals and register for those Illumineer Quest events, and be aware, now is the time to start calling your locals to ask about presales on Hyperia City - Ravensburger Playhub stores should be getting confirmation of their allocations soon.

Slowking Deck Guide (Pokémon TCG)

Slowking is a real player now, but there's more than one way to play it!

By Natalie Millar

|@nataliem9999
|

Published Sep 22, 2026

|

5 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series: Pokémon Deck Guides

Hello everyone! Slowking has been a strong deck for quite some time in the Pokémon TCG, and it's looking like it will be gaining a new card from the 30th Celebration set. Seek Inspiration is such a dramatic attack to use when you flip the top card of your deck, and you get to use some of the most powerful attacks in the format. Slowking also has a strong time against Dragapult ex decks, which make it a very appealing choice currently!

Slowking Deck Guide

The core strategy of this deck is to use Slowking's Seek Inspiration as a sort of toolbox, but you're mostly copying Kyurem's Trifrost attack to wipe your opponent's board in the early game. 110 damage is usually enough to clear off most Stage 1 Pokémon, which makes going first so strong with this deck since you have two turns to draw into the Trifrost. You use Academy at Night to set up the Pokémon on the top of your deck, and also have Wondrous Patch to attach extra Energy during your turn and Boomerang Energy to help with chaining Trifrosts.

This deck also gets to use the powerful Telepathic Psychic Energy to get out extra Slowpokes and Latias ex for mobility. Since we have easy access to Latias ex, we also get to use Mega Kangaskhan ex for its Run Errand ability. Drawing into the Slowking, two Energy, the attacker and the Academy at Night is a lot to ask for and having a low maintenance draw engine is really useful. Mega Kangaskhan fits this bill, and is especially strong against Itchy Pollen, which many Dragapult decks try to use to slow down your Trifrost.

There are also four copies of Ciphermaniac's Codebreaking in this deck to help with finding specific cards. You can draw them straight away with Run Errand or just leave them on top to draw them later. Notably, you can also stack your attacker on top and bypass the need for Academy at Night. The rest of this deck's engine is just the standard Meowth ex and Fezandipiti ex consistency Pokémon, as well as a Lillie's Clefairy ex to let you hit Dragapult ex for weakness and as an alternate attacker if all your Slowpokes go down. I chose to go with Secret Box as the ACE SPEC for this deck since it grabs almost the whole attack with the Supporter, Tool and Stadium options.

The attackers in this decklist are relatively simple. There are two copies of Kyurem for the Trifrost attack and two copies of Metagross for Metallic Hammer. Due to a quirk in the rules, you're allowed to deal the extra damage with Metallic Hammer despite not having any Metal Energy on the Metagross - you don't even have to discard anything to deal 300! Against decks with lots of small Pokémon, you'll usually go with Trifrost, and against anything with bigger Pokémon, you'll primarily use Metagross. The core strategy of this deck is relatively high maintenance and often doesn't allow for you to any gust cards outside of maybe Prime Catcher, so having Zeraora's Thunder Raid attack as a way to close out the game against a benched Fezandipiti ex or Meowth ex is very strong.

Unown is the newest card from 30th Celebration for this deck and I think it has a lot of utility. Mysterious Signal deals with Budew for two Prize cards, kicking off the Prize trade, and can also KO Dreepy for two Prize cards. Trifrost does sort of accomplish the same purpose, but at this point in the format, most Dragapult players will start off the game slightly underbenching against Slowking. Unown is a great response to this as you put on pressure with the Prize trade and they can't rely on trapping your Slowking active since it doesn't discard Energy.

There is a copy of Surfer in this deck to act as an additional switching card. After using Trifrost, Slowking sometimes ends up trapped active, especially if you don't have a Boomerang Energy attached. This deck does include Switch but Surfer is an additional switching card and acts as a bad draw supporter in a pinch. Night Stretcher is also a very strong card in this deck, but there are only two copies currently. You usually have enough resources to close out the game if you use the Night Stretchers correctly, but even still I think that including a third copy would be nice.

Notably when up against single-Prize decks that include Shaymin, this deck massively struggles. You can't Trifrost early which removes a significant part of your game plan, and this deck cannot really set up more than four attackers whereas the other single-Prize decks can easily use six attackers throughout the game. The Slowking deck doesn't really work if the Slowkings only take one Prize each, which is why the below version of the deck sometimes sees play.

Against decks that use single-Prize smaller attackers, you can use Drapion's Hazardous Tail to paralyze them, then use Mysterious Signal to take the two-Prize KO. You also have access to Munkidori to move that Drapion recoil damage over to your opponent's board, and Crispin to get additional Energy onto your board. This deck has significantly more options than the other Slowking deck, but it's less consistent and generally worse at the primary game plan. A lot of players do prefer the additional options and wider game plans though, and you can play tons of alternate attackers such as Annihilape SSP, Annihilape PBL, Zoroark WHT and Cofagrigus SSP

There are a ton of ways to build the Slowking deck and multiple ways to answer problematic matchups. Playing the straightforward version will result in your deck executing its strategy more often, but with more techs you have wider game plan. Good luck if you choose to play this deck, and hopefully there are no Shaymins in sight!

Flesh and Blood was named as such because of its dedication to in-store play. It's a game that harkens back to both the formative nineties of the modern local game store and the ever-increasing need for a third space in the modern day. This dedication is woven into the very foundation of Legend Story Studios mission statement:  

"Our mission is to bring people together in the Flesh and Blood through the common language of playing great games"

You are supposed to play in the flesh and blood. It was important — should still be important — to sit down opposite friend or stranger alike to sling spells and trade cards over a cold beverage or three. In fact, retailers must operate a "bricks and mortar gaming store with table space available for customers to play games" to be eligible for product in the first place.  

These stores are the lifeblood of the Flesh and Blood community and TCGplayer wants to be sure that we're actively supporting these sellers as part of our larger partnership with the team at Legend Story Studios. That's why we're introducing GEM Store Badges to the TCGplayer marketplace. 

GEM Store Badges are an expansion of TCGplayer's trusted seller program framework, helping to strengthen buyer confidence when purchasing products and assist shoppers in discovering reputable Flesh and Blood sellers on the platform.  

Eligible sellers will have the option to display a dedicated GEM logo next to all of their listings on the marketplace, helping you to find retailers who are not only trusted by Legend Story Studios, but are running Organized Play Events, providing welcoming, consistent in-store experiences and actively supporting the growth of their local communities.  

As a buyer, you'll be able to see this badge as a filter (in List View) when shopping on TCGplayer. If you're browsing for a specific item, you'll be able to filter product pages for GEM badges or spot them next to seller feedback too! 

Join us in supporting GEM Store retailers today: Click here to browse Flesh and Blood Usurp the Shadow Throne products and try out the new filters for yourself! Happy shopping!
